selected_passages.title: raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.title: sources/Apple_defends_Google_Search_deal_in_court_There_wasn_t_a_valid_alternative
selected_passages.text:
- The trial is titled US v. Google.
- Eddy Cue is a witness for Apple.
- Judge Amit Mehta presided over the case.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) has been in place since 2002.
- Cue negotiated the current ISA iteration in 2016.
- Google CEO Sundar Pichai was involved in the 2016 renegotiation.
- Meagan Bellshaw is a Justice Department lawyer.
- John Schmidtlein is a Google lawyer.
- Three iPhone screenshots were shown regarding setup process.
- Screenshots included the Appearance screen, location-tracking prompt, and App Tracking Transparency pop-up.
- DuckDuckGo's CEO testified previously claiming switching search engines takes too many steps.
- Safari was introduced in early 2003.
- Before 2003, users had to manually type google.com to search.
- Apple deals with Yahoo and Bing to make those services easy to find.
- The ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits.
- Specific revenue numbers were discussed in closed court sessions.
- Google pays Apple billions of dollars a year.
- Apple believes it has better privacy than Google.
- The ISA requires Google to allow searching without logging in.
- Apple makes it harder for Google to track users via Safari.
- The courtroom had a monitor malfunction during testimony.
- Judge Mehta joked about Apple making a donation if they wanted to switch.
- Cue stated Apple would never consider walking away from the deal if revenue share couldn't be agreed upon.
- Cue claimed he couldn't remember the names of some search engine alternatives.

selected_passages.text:
- Eddy Cue testified that there was no valid alternative to Google Search for Apple devices at the time of the deal.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) makes Google the default search engine on Apple products in exchange for billions in payments.
- Apple believes in protecting user privacy but also maintains a strong partnership with Google, creating a central tension in the trial.
- Cue argued that showing users alternative search engines during setup would degrade the user experience and slow down device onboarding.
- The Justice Department questions whether Apple's choice of Google is based on product quality or financial incentives.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: Grey herself is a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google. She admits that she may have misinterpreted the evidence, but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. So what does Google say? In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/Is_Google_Search_better_than_the_rest_And_is_that_fair
selected_passages.text: For the US, which has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, this legal case could be an uphill battle. But for the rest of us, it offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share. Is it still focused on being the best? Or, as has been alleged, does it use its ubiquity to squeeze us for money even at the expense of product quality? How ‘organic’ are Google’s results? This month, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray, which alleged that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people’s search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”. Loading Google rejected this in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards, but the degree to which it was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google’s part. A suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times.

In a post on X, Google’s official search liaison, Danny Sullivan, said ad systems do not affect the organic results, i.e. the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored. “Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads. A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query,” he said. “It’s no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning ... If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that’s not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren’t even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help.” It is true that some search queries result in more ads than others, and what ads you get can vary wildly depending on your request, which is the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads. But Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.
